最高难度下，依旧继承《亚瑟王骑士传说》的垃圾数值，纯粹的堆伤害+限制你的回复量，毫无策略性可言。 有人发评测说上来选粗暴难度被打死怪谁，这是来阴阳我的是吧？我就选粗暴难度怎么了？而且我还粗暴通关了怎么了？我说他难度只会堆数值没错吧？怎么了？有问题吗？只会堆数值增加难度的战棋就是垃圾战棋，怎么了？还不能说了？非要舔这个制作组你才高兴？臭傻逼 接着中文翻译不全，并且缺字、漏字、语句不通顺。我不知道开发组这个解决能多难，发售几天了，通关了还没见到补丁。 本作就是《亚瑟王骑士传说》的DLC，改成了完整游戏拿来卖，系统玩法什么都是阉割版，毫无诚意。 我是《亚瑟王骑士传说》1代出的时候就买了，这次《第九军团》出了也是第一时间买，感觉被喂屎。 虽然价格不贵，但是这样下去，你们的亚瑟王IP要毁在你们手里。

Generally when you play a dlc or a second game in a series, or whatever this is, you expect the original idea to be expanded upon and improved, not dumbed down... there are fewer features, and its just doesn't feel like it deserves to be given the "king arthur" title... literally ervery aspect of the game was made weaker... the ultimate skills are not even that interesting... like they are cool abilities but the system for unlocking them is entirely uninspired.... making them feel less ultimate and more bland. Even the side missions are not side missions... you literally have to complete most of them to unlock the next story mission anyway. The list of things that have been dumbed down instead of improved- No injury system or lasting damage no character management, recruit the 6 chars and play with all 6 every level, except the levels that exclude one, but thats not a choice to make, its just a level quirk skill/level ups is far simpler and everything starts unlocked, except some of the 1 point improvements. town management and titles are a snore. no laws, just decrees town management resources are very plentiful and its a matter of what order to unlock things, no hard sacrifices need be made to unlock everything, just kinda gonna happen eventually experience is non existent, everyone levels every map. no meaningful choices to be made during the maps... there is an obvious right and wrong choice every time "get bonus treasure or be a ♥♥♥♥ to this person offering you bonus treasure and get nothing" is not a choice loot simply is... it doesn't get better as the game progresses, you just get more of it to choose between. from 5 weapon types and 3 armor types to 3 and 2. this really feels like the game that would have been made BEFORE knights tale and evolved into knights tale, not the other way around

2022's King Arthur: Knight's Tale, which wasn't about King Arthur and wasn't a knight's tale, was a fundamentally good strategy/tactics game utterly ruined by really, really bad level design, totally bloated beyond belief from a solid 15ish hour RPG to an unbelievable 30+ hour slog. Its missions were way too long, its encounters were way too samey, and there hadn't been nearly enough thought put into the totality of the campaign experience. The much shorter Legion IX promised to fix those issues, and having now beaten it (in about 7 hours, or maybe more like 6), I can report that it mostly has. Legion IX features vastly improved encounter design over the base game. The missions are way shorter (thank Jupiter). The encounters are way better designed; enemies no longer spawn in behind you magically, and there are now sometimes objectives to complete beyond homicide. The cast has been shrunk to six, but you always get six (or five) on a mission, rather than four; this is a great change. Characters have simpler and smaller skill trees. Knight's Tale had a bad story, with bad writing and very bad dialogue. Legion IX is way worse on both counts. But its gameplay is mostly improved. It's paced better, plays, better, and is definitely more fun. But it has lost something by stripping so much out. The simplification of base building is a shame, and while I think it was a good choice to remove the permadeath/injury mechanics, both thematically and mechanically, they haven't been replaced with anything. It feels like something is missing. I also miss the length of the skill trees. I thought they were too long last time, given the number of characters at your disposal, but with only six, these characters didn't seem to have nearly enough abilities.I managed to afford mostly everything, and where I put my points barely seemed to matter. As for the characters themselves, Mento is insanely OP--good--but the Flamen idiot has to be intentionally worthless, because I never found any use for him at all. He's a total joke, with a kit that makes no sense and feels underbaked. The Praetorian is similarly almost useless, because he lacks the mobility that Mordred and other characters had in the last game, and enemies almost never walk into his defensive spells. But the gameplay is still fun. It's tactically engaging while also tactile and satisfying. The worst thing about Knight's Tale was that it was too long. The worst thing about Legion Ix might be that it's too short. After two years, I had expected more. I haven't finished everything yet; after the credits roll, it's promised that the TRUE final boss is still forthcoming. I'll probably get to him eventually, but where I am now, my progress does feel kind of stagnant. Every quest I finish, a new one pops up, like I'm playing the Spooky Scary Roman Skeleton version of whack-a-mole with my pilum. If you're like me and enjoyed Knight's Tale but for its encounter design, I do recommend Legion IX. It's reasonably priced and decent fun. Just don't bother with the story, because the dialogue is really, truly horrible. Edit: I played a bit more in the post-game, and it's a huge treadmill. I'm not enjoying it at all.

Compared to A Knight's Tale, it isn't as good. It is cheaper, but that is because it's shorter. I got 5 missions in and it just doesn't feel as immersive or dark as A Knight's Tale. There's also no voice acting when selecting missions anymore. Was hoping for that same quality in the immersion/sound department. Everything else is more or less the same mechanically with the exception that your party members no longer have vitality/can die as they are proper undead like The Lost in the series.

This is hard, considering the game is 18 bucks, then I have to cut it some slack, the fact that the first game is also 18 bucks and has 10X the content, also moves me towards a "no". First game had 6ish cinematics, this one has 0. Voice acting was pretty good on the first game, this one is pretty bad, lol. The storyline was awesome and kept me wanting to know more, this one didn't even really have a story, you just went around and killed everyone as an undead roman soldier, while your two biggest advisers just bicker against each other. You will have to choose between one of the two "Seers/magic users" and there is no choice, you will lose one. You also only get 6 characters, which is a full group, and in some missions one of the two magic users won't come with, so you are using a team that is missing a character. This is the whole game too. The first game had, I think 10-12 characters? Which gave a lot more variety. When the character leaves your group for good , you don't get any of the relics or items that they were equipped with, not even after you kill them later on. :( Townbuilding is pretty bad, most of the upgrades are useless, it costs a lot and you get stuff like "Potions are cheaper, potions cost no AP. Scrolls are cheaper, scrolls cost 0 AP". So that is 4 upgrades, So 4k gold and 4k building materials. Using a potion or scroll only costs 1 AP - totally not worth the upgrade cost, the potions are cheap and you end up getting a lot of potions/scrolls per mission. The statues (They give 1 buff and 1 negative) are pretty bad, I only used the one that gives me vitality with each attack, but the resting area will not allow me to heal my vitality, only to fix my armor. The other ones are just not worth it. When you beat the game and get like "New end game missions" well, you still only have 5 our of 6 characters..so never a full team. I really loved the first game, disappointed in this one.

亚瑟王骑士传说的老玩家路过，原作玩了200多个小时，超级上头。 这个新作玩了一会儿，感觉挺好玩的，目前为止没有遇到什么汉化很大的问题，虽然有些缺陷，但是大致能看明白。 原作的汉化更过分，经过了差不多1年多才修复好汉化。 这作简化了很多，感觉比前作玩起来轻松，我不需要考虑命源的损伤，不需要考虑受伤的问题，这其实是一个进步。 前作受伤治疗确实太折磨人了。 角色BUILD还是一如既往的有趣，你想玩什么流派都可以 角色我感觉并不需要很多，前作因为有受伤问题所以需要替补，这作并不需要，所以这不是缺点 其他的改动不多，50多块钱的价格已经很优惠了，我个人还是觉得很值得的， 希望差评不要太影响销量，游戏是好游戏，适合小众的战棋爱好者 缺点：人物太丑，跑步太慢，优化有点问题开4K很卡
玩第一作就行，这作一坨，短的令人窒息，给人的感觉就是灵感来了，做了个开头，然后后面就不想做了，直接结束。

TLDR - Get it on a Sale. The best way to describe this game is, "Expeditions Rome Undead Nightmare" the story is essentially every Ermor game in Dominions VI, with undead Romans and all. When i first brought this game i was like, "Oh a game where you fight Undead Romans, that neat." Then i realized that I get to play as the Undead Romans i was instantly drawn to it. However. The game is increadibly underwhelming, the story it's self is actually really intresting, however it it horribly told. You playing as some dead relative of Gaius Julius Ceasar that also happens to also be a redditor, during the entire game he just makes ♥♥♥♥♥♥ puns and autistic comments, Your party consists of your Discord VC Stalker that never contributes nothing to the conversation, another discord autist that has a copy of books that you should not own, a non virgin virgin thot and this ramdom dude that crawls out of hell and contributes nothing to the story, which is weird considering the way he was introduced to the story, and to top it all off, all these interesting personalities are all AI voice acted, so you can imagine how the conversations go. The whole plot is that you're a bunch of undead romans, who even in death cannot escape the american military draft, they are summoned by this ramdon guy that somehow holds the title of Emperor even in Hellenic Hell, i guess that's a common occurance down there, anyways, you're asked to somehow find a way out of hell, of which you do, ofc not in game, cause that totally would not be something interesting to do in game, anyway you escape Hellenic Hell to arrive the British Heaven of Avalon also known as Hell for anyone who isn't native to the British Isles, which is understatement which that the first people you meet in there are the average Scotish Nationalist, after that for some reason you find a Roman Colony in Avalon, and from there on out you have to conquer the land in the name of Rome! Except you don't, the entire game is you just killing homeless people and a bunch of Arturians knights, Merlin shows up once or twice, hes a wimp and is easily beaten, You can either be every Roman that is represented in the media in the 20th century or Simp, there is no where in between, this is convoluted and makes no sense to whoever is reading this but trust me those are the only two options. Gameplay is mid and most of the classes are that interesting, the Story is the strongest part of the game it is actually intesting, however it feels like it is being told by someone who is hosting his first DnD game, and instead of running a a premade game by the Grand Wizards of the Coast, they instead take 3 months working on a their own OC world based off their real life counterparts, and it's Lore and Story is told in such way as well. So yeah, don't buy this game unless it is on Sale, and remember Hoes are temporary the Glory of Rome is Eternal.

Short version: Is it as good as the first game? No. Is it still enjoyable? Yes. The long version: as many others have mentioned here, Legion IX seems like a step backwards from Knight's Tale. A large amount of mechanics have been removed, the writing and voice acting are noticeably worse, and almost all the maps are copy-pasted from the first game. It might be best to think of this game as a DLC or very extensive mod. If you felt that the first game was too complicated, then this was made for you. If not, then you might be somewhat annoyed by the dumbing-down of the mechanics here. Positives and new mechanics: -Each character has unique abilities with no overlap. -Added the Larium, which applies significant modifiers to game mechanics. -The character that wields a two-handed weapon no longer feels so immobile as to be useless. -The "archer" has much better damage output and is now actually competitive. Overall, classes feel much more balanced. Negatives and removed mechanics: -No more roster management. Most missions are played with the same 5 characters. Some missions have a 6th. -Gear no longer has levels. An item gained in the first 5 missions could still be viable in the final mission. Instead, you can invest resources to upgrade a weapon or armor piece once. -Maximum character level is reduced to 18. -HP is no longer a major mechanic. It's now just armor and vitality, unless you use an ability for temporary HP. -No more lasting injuries or resting between missions. -The morality chart is now a morality line. Just plain good and evil.

有一说一，太短了，而且玩法也比较一般，内容也不是很充实，但是设定这方面可太炫酷了，是我喜欢的类型，然而这样一个炫酷的设定却没能做出来一个好的剧情，更是让我有一点失望，但是不影响我给个好评。 其他的方面就不说了，单论剧情方面我个人感觉还可以有很多的扩展。比如第九军团是怎么从冥界逃过塔尔塔洛斯的？这一段经历到底是怎样的？皇帝苏拉是怎样的一个人？同僚的经历如何？这些都没有体现，以至于整个游玩体验非常单薄，让我感觉我不是在玩《亚瑟王：第九军团》，而是一个随处可见的战旗游戏。 如果要我来说，在这样的一个设定下，剧情应该最少有三个章节。（剧透预警） 第一章，门托和他的军团被苏拉集结，他们需要设法离开冥界，躲过塔尔塔洛斯的追击，在这里主角会遇到军团的同僚以及恶魔线的指引人涅涅，在这一章要专注于描绘军团效仿奥德修斯和埃涅阿斯这些先贤进行一次属于永恒罗马的新奥德赛，并且向玩家展示苏拉本人的魅力，给他们未来选择恶魔线一个足够充分的理由。 第二章，是在逃离了塔尔塔洛斯的追击之后，主角找到各处分散的军团同僚，并且见到人类线的指引人火女，在这一章也就是如今游戏内的内容，需要让玩家了解苏拉的另一面，并且看到第九军团如果来到阿瓦隆，这里会变成什么样子，给玩家选择人类线一个理由，并且在这一章也可以让玩家和前作主角团进行一些碰撞和交流。 第三章也就是选择人类/恶魔线之后，双方进行的战争。可以选择忠于皇帝，在阿瓦隆建立新罗马；也可以选择成为圆桌骑士的一员，对抗暴君苏拉；甚至还可以在走人类线的基础上杀死火女，独立于圆桌骑士和第九军团，成为第三方势力（其实就是我个人认为人类线压根就不是建立永恒罗马，而是看卡梅洛的脸色吃饭，毕竟最后的剧情里面骑士给我的感觉太傲慢了。。。） 在这些基础上加一些新的玩法和机制，并且在人类线和恶魔线做出各自的差异，比如人类线可以同时使用叛变的主角和圆桌骑士，恶魔线可以策反/腐化部分圆桌骑士并且可以奴役神明（指睡神和独眼之神）之类的。 目前游戏内容给我的感觉就是一个小型的dlc，把这么有趣的设定完全浪费了，希望未来还会有一些补丁或者新内容

It looks like there was a contest of who can came up with the most idiotic mask and the winners made it to the team. To add insult to injury we are suppose to fight and kill our own heroes from the previous game, you know, the ones we actually like and care about. Still, regardless of what you decide, the result is "whatever" as it doesn't change anything. Next time instead of trying to come up with a really creative idea just give us normal roman soldiers doing normal roman soldier things and I promise you it's gonna be a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ banger. Also, stop simplifing things. We, players who like your games, are not ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ idiots. If you're trying to appeal to idiots stop doing turn-based to begin with.

I'd love to be able to recommend this game, but I can't - it's just too short. The turn-based combat is great! The story is engaging to start with and the character levelling and loot are great, but I finished the main campaign in 8 hours! After that there are no more characters to be found, no more levels to be gained and almost all the loot you find is useless because you already have the best loot available. There's lots more content, but it is just an endless parade of repetitive, rather pointless side quests. I gave up a few hours later.

In all seriousness though, I like the gameplay and the universe but it's a game I won't finish. I don't want to do the side mission "Bleak Coves", and there is no new main mission after Reckoning. King Arthur: A Knight's Tale (KT) ended up being one of my favorite games of that year -- and one of the very few games I have 100+ hours in. This stand-alone expansion hits all the same notes, and I enjoyed it thoroughly. For reference, I paid full retail for both titles, and got my money's worth. Same combat, same setting as KT -- but from a different angle. The music, one of my stand-out favorites from KT that I still listen to on Spotify, has some tracks about as solid here...perhaps a bit less, but not by much. The voice acting in this installment is below the quality of the mainline KT, but hey -- this is a much cheaper expansion...so that is understandable. All-in-all, this is well worth playing -- I really love what this company has been doing with their titles!
Simplified gameplay and bad voice acting are sore points for this follow up to the brillant King Arthur: Knight's Tale. I expectped much bettr from this team.

First of all, let me start by saying that this is a good game which does quite a lot of things very well. I don’t regret buying it. I am happy to have it in my library. Yet, unfortunately, it has a few cardinal sins that personally are dealbreakers for me. And because of that, I won’t finish it. Let me also add that I haven’t played the Camelot prequel to this game. At first glance, it looked pretty similar to Expeditions Rome. Which I liked very much. Combat, storytelling, gameplay, in all aspects. The story is interesting enough, a lost Roman legion ordered to find an escape from hell ends up in some sort of purgatory land in between the two worlds. The main 3 characters are very well drawn out, they are easy to grow fond of despite the fact that they’re ugly-as-hell skeleton warriors from, well, hell. The first missions were promising where I was trying to figure out the game&combat mechanics. Then, just as I thought I had a grasp of the game, the overworld map came up. I was looking at my possibilities. I kept looking. For a while. Until I was convinced that it was not my dumb ass missing anything, but the whole game was a strictly linear, scripted theme park ride. Zero chance to swerve away. None. OK, not all games need to be open world. I’m not expecting Fallout- or Avernum- or Underrail-style unnerving sense of deadly freedom from all games. That’d be unfair. But let me at least roam around a bit to freely get my ass kicked in the wrong times&places. Instead, it turned out to be a RPG-lite very much like Mutant Year Zero and Miasma Chronicles where the whole game is a scripted series of mini maps in which exploration is just a formality, a dull matter of not stepping on the wrong tile (the dangerous, combat-initiating tiles are marked red anyway) until you clear the fog and “discover” your 3 options: Frontal attack (wrong option), the weak spot (correct option) and sometimes a third more adventurous opening. Some battles have no optional approach, you just have to take them head-on. The maps are designed to give you a couple of different paths to the final objective. Well, there you have it, a choice to make. There’s no inventory. Well, there’s one, but you can’t access it during missions. That’s… an unfortunate game design decision in my book. Undead legionaries cracking jokes while swinging blades and spells in a fantasy land, but they’re unable to exchange a few items and potions between them. You can’t use any of your abilities outside combat. Why? I don’t know. Speaking of choices, they’re mostly confined to your character builds and base building department of the game. Paying 500 gold for a merchant upgrade to buy cheaper potions, wow, that’s what I call exciting RPG decision making. Let me repeat, characters and skills are quite well done. To the point that they really made me want to play on, until complete linearity choked my will to live. I think the mutated duck game is based on a table top game, so that would explain its limitations. But why follow such an example… I guess there’s a considerable gamer segment who like RPG-lites. The game is very nice in some aspects, leading undead legionaries is really cool, and I wish the developers well, but know before buying that in my book, this is not a CRPG, or even an RPG for that matter. If you liked Knight's Tale and are looking for more of the same from this, your disappointment will be immeasurable and your day will be ruined. It's less and it's worse. It's a much lesser game than the original in every aspect. It re-uses levels and assets, except making them worse - for example there was a maze level, that I actually got lost in while playing the original, but in this it's just a corridor, there's literally only 1 way to go. Which brings me to the next point - it's much more linear. The original wasn't exactly an open-ended experience itself, but there were different missions to take at any given time, divergent paths, levels could be navigated differently and combats started at different spots. Here you're on rails 99% of the time in all those aspects. Character, gear and base progression also feel worse and more boring. It feels like it throws more relics at me, but they're less exciting and rarely an upgrades, so I just end up dusting most of them. Even putting comparisons to the original to the side, even on its own it's an annoying experience. It's mind-numbingly easy until all of a sudden it becomes damn near impossible and then back to easy. Compounding that is the tiny roster that's just enough to fill out a full party, but the game constantly makes one or another hero unavailable for missions for no other obvious reason than to annoy the player, limiting their tactical options further. In short, gameplay is tedious and annoying. And narrative isn't making up for it either. It's serviceable at best and again, worse than the original

A great spin-off from Neocore's King Arthur: Knight's Tale. Has a LOT of the same systems and whatnot but it is decidedly smaller in scope and narrative. So far though, having a great time. Even though it's smaller in scope don't get it twisted. This game STILL has a LOT of deep systems, characters and possibilities. You can play on "Normal" or "Roguelite" mode. With Roguelite there's NO saving, just autosaves and every decision is permanent. In "normal" you can scum save til your heart's content. The characters, the world and the story is really well done. The ONLY issue I really have with the game is the voice overs for the characters. It seems a LOT of the characters just phoned in their performance and it's not that awesome to listen to them speak most times. Still, the story is interesting and well done so there is that. Neocore has created some absolute gems over their sorted history. The OG King Arthur "Role Playing Games" were pretty awesome back in the day. Then they created the Van Helsing trilogy which was just awesome on every single level for an action rpg. Then they created Warhammer 40k Prophecy and Martyr. Prophecy stumbled immensely at launch. Many systems were just not fun and the loot was paltry at best. However, with patches, updates and Martyr released they fixed it into a HUGE and ENORMOUS game with lots of complex systems, loot, characters and game play options. I'm def looking forward to seeing what Neocore does next as they're one of my favorite smaller dev groups that make some great games. This one included. Oh, you SHOULD go buy King Arthur Knight's Tale. It's awesome.

While I really liked the base game I cannot recommend this "expansion". It doesn't offer you anything new, it's short and repeats the mistakes of it's predecessor. The artistic direction is fine but it kinda clashes with the avalonian style. You fight knights in ornate gothic armor in old roman cuirasses and sandals. Tanky enemies, overwhelming numbers, mechanics that prolong fights etc. It's not uncommon to be outnumbered 3 or even 4 to 1. While doable this really feels like a needless time waster. Of course there are some weird difficulty spikes. Especially towards the end. It's very short. Around 10 hours if you want to beat it. In the end I would not recommend this even on a sale. It brings nothing of value to the base game, it's really short, barebones and annoying. Honestly this should have been a bigger DLC for the original game instead of a stand alone. I regret my purchase.

Personally, I don't care much for Roman lore, I always found it sort of vain and uninspiring compared to their predecessors, the Greeks, or to other pagan lore from the time when the Romans scoured Europe. But that only makes me respect this sort of standalone DLC to the previous King Arthur even more. I'll explain. The game is mostly the same turn-based extravaganza, with many build options and discoverable synergies, the main difference being the said lore. This time, they even threw something extra on the top in the fashion of light riddling (word riddles, architectonic puzzles, torches / hidden walls / hidden objects manipulation, etc.). Not anything overdone, just an elegant icing on the cake. It's also a somewhat smaller game than its predecessor, where the smaller really means just a lower amount of heroes, and less extensive hero's upkeep (no wounds healing system). But that still amounts to a fair 30-40 hours of gameplay in the same, gritty atmosphere which steadilly seeps into every corner around you as soon as you load the game up. So, for the price they put it up for, it's an absolute steal of a TB game, and a solid piece of development craft. Heartily recomended.

King Arthur: Legion IX delivers an engaging standalone tactical RPG that expands the dark fantasy universe of King Arthur: Knight's Tale through the introduction of an entirely new faction and storyline. Developed and published by NeocoreGames, the game follows Gaius Julius Mento, a tribune of the legendary Ninth Legion who is resurrected in the mystical realm of Avalon. Rather than retelling familiar Arthurian legends, the campaign explores the ambitions of a Roman commander determined to establish a new empire within a land ruled by magic, mythical creatures, and ancient curses. This fresh perspective gives the expansion its own identity while remaining faithful to the grim atmosphere and mature storytelling that define the series. The narrative is built around the Roman Legion's struggle to survive and conquer Avalon, creating a fascinating blend of Roman history and Arthurian mythology. As Gaius Julius Mento attempts to build Nova Roma, players encounter rival armies, monstrous beasts, corrupted knights, and supernatural threats that constantly challenge their progress. The story successfully balances military conquest with personal ambition, allowing players to experience a campaign driven by determination, loyalty, and the desire to restore the glory of a fallen civilization. While the plot is more focused than that of the original game, it remains consistently engaging thanks to strong world-building and memorable encounters. Combat continues to be the centerpiece of the experience, offering highly strategic turn-based battles where every action matters. Victory depends on careful positioning, efficient use of action points, skill combinations, and exploiting enemy weaknesses rather than relying on overwhelming force. Each battlefield encourages tactical thinking by presenting varied enemy types, environmental hazards, and mission objectives that require adaptability. The Roman-themed heroes introduce fresh combat styles and abilities, ensuring that battles feel distinct from those found in the base game while preserving the satisfying tactical depth that fans expect. Character progression is another highlight, with each recruit possessing unique skills, specialization options, and equipment choices. Players gradually strengthen their legion by unlocking powerful abilities, discovering better gear, and customizing heroes to suit different combat strategies. Building an effective team involves balancing offensive damage, defensive capabilities, crowd control, healing, and mobility, rewarding thoughtful planning throughout the campaign. The progression system remains meaningful because every upgrade noticeably improves a character's effectiveness, encouraging experimentation with different party compositions. Outside of combat, the game introduces settlement management through the construction and expansion of Nova Roma. Developing the city provides practical benefits such as improved resources, stronger infrastructure, and additional support for future expeditions. Although these management mechanics are not overly complex, they provide a satisfying sense of long-term progression that complements the tactical gameplay. Watching the Roman settlement gradually grow reinforces the campaign's central theme of rebuilding an empire within an unfamiliar and hostile world. The presentation effectively captures the dark fantasy tone of Avalon. Environments are richly detailed, blending Roman architecture with medieval ruins, haunted forests, cursed battlefields, and mystical landscapes that constantly remind players of the world's supernatural nature. Character models are well designed, spell animations are visually impressive, and combat effects remain clear even during large-scale encounters. Combined with atmospheric lighting and strong environmental design, every location contributes to the game's oppressive yet captivating atmosphere. The sound design further enhances immersion through a dramatic orchestral soundtrack that shifts naturally between moments of exploration and intense combat. Weapon impacts, magical abilities, and creature sounds all deliver satisfying audio feedback, while the voice performances help establish the personalities and motivations of the central characters. Together, the music and sound effects strengthen the emotional weight of the story and make each battle feel appropriately epic. Although Legion IX is marketed as a standalone adventure, its campaign is naturally smaller than the original King Arthur: Knight's Tale. Players looking for an expansive epic with dozens of hours of content may find its shorter length somewhat limiting. However, the focused scope allows the game to maintain a consistently high level of quality without relying on unnecessary filler. Every mission introduces meaningful objectives, challenging encounters, or narrative developments that keep the experience engaging from beginning to end. King Arthur: Legion IX succeeds because it builds upon an already strong tactical foundation while introducing enough original ideas to justify its existence as more than a simple expansion. Its compelling Roman-inspired storyline, rewarding tactical combat, satisfying progression systems, and atmospheric presentation combine to create an experience that will appeal to strategy enthusiasts and fans of dark fantasy alike. Even though its campaign is more concise than the main game, the quality of its gameplay and storytelling makes it a worthwhile addition to the King Arthur universe. Rating: 7/10
